title: Did the New Deal Work?
objective: After this level you can weigh the case that the New Deal rescued the country against the cases that it fell short or went too far.
summary: Output recovered by 1937, but unemployment stayed above 10 percent until World War II. The Liberty League said the New Deal did too much; Huey Long said too little.

cards.headline: Did the New Deal work? Americans were arguing about it while it happened.
cards.body: Some said it went too far, others that it didn’t go far enough. Historians still weigh the same record.

cards.headline: The starting line
cards.body: When Franklin D. Roosevelt took office on March 4, 1933, the banking system had collapsed and nearly 25 percent of the labor force was unemployed. Picture one in every four workers with no job to go to. Roosevelt’s answer, the New Deal, poured out programs, some built to last, like Social Security in 1935.

cards.headline: The case that it worked
cards.body: Defenders point to a fast rebound. Richard A. Walker of the Living New Deal writes that by 1937 the recovery had pushed output, income and manufacturing back to 1929 levels. In four years, the economy had climbed out of the hole it fell into after the crash. For its defenders, that is a rescue.

cards.headline: Too far, or not far enough?
cards.body: Critics came from both sides at once. In August 1934 conservatives organized the American Liberty League, arguing Roosevelt had done too much and accusing him of creeping socialism. From the other direction, Senator Huey Long of Louisiana said the New Deal did not do enough. In 1934 he founded the Share Our Wealth Society to limit big fortunes and guarantee every family a minimum.

cards.headline: The fact everyone must explain
cards.body: Here is the stubborn part. Unemployment stayed above 10 percent through the New Deal years, and only World War II brought full employment. Defenders point to the rebound. Critics on the right say government grew too much; critics on the left say it did too little. Your verdict depends on the yardstick you choose.

questions.prompt: Which group, formed in August 1934, argued that Roosevelt had done too much?

options.label: The Share Our Wealth Society
options.rationale: Huey Long’s group said the New Deal did too little.

options.label: The Sons of Liberty
options.rationale: They opposed the Stamp Act in 1765.

options.label: The NAACP
options.rationale: The NAACP was a civil rights organization (Level 67).

questions.explanation: Conservatives organized the American Liberty League in August 1934, accusing Roosevelt of creeping socialism.

questions.prompt: Which fact do both the New Deal’s defenders and its critics have to explain?

options.label: Unemployment stayed above 10 percent until World War II
Output never recovered in the 1930s
options.rationale: Output was back to 1929 levels by 1937.

options.label: Unemployment was low when Roosevelt took office
Social Security was repealed in 1937
options.rationale: Social Security was created in 1935 and was not repealed.

questions.explanation: Output recovered, but unemployment stayed above 10 percent until the war brought full employment: a fact any verdict must account for.

questions.prompt: Josephson and Nevins read the same Gilded Age record in opposite ways (Level 64). Which pair judged the New Deal from opposite sides?

options.label: The American Liberty League and Huey Long
Andrew Carnegie and John D. Rockefeller
options.rationale: They were Gilded Age industrialists, not New Deal critics.

options.label: William Lloyd Garrison and Frederick Douglass
options.rationale: They argued about the Constitution and slavery (Level 33).

questions.explanation: The Liberty League said the New Deal did too much; Huey Long said it did too little: one program, opposite verdicts.
